title: The Caliph al-Maamun and the Pyramids

keywords: the caliph al-maamun and the pyramids
full_text:
The Abbasid Caliph Al-Ma'mun, famous for his passion for mathematics, astronomy, and the translation of ancient Greek and Persian manuscripts, arrived in Egypt with a great retinue of engineers, scholars, and masons. Standing before the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Caliph looked upon its colossal limestone bulk, rising like a mountain against the azure desert sky.

Legend claimed that within the pyramid rested the secret scrolls of ancient sciences, celestial charts of forgotten astrologers, and immense treasures of gold accumulated by the pharaohs before the great flood.

Determined to unlock its mysteries, Al-Ma'mun ordered his stonemasons to breach the northern face of the monument. For six months, hundreds of workmen heated the hard stone with roaring fires of wood and cracked the boiling limestone with cold vinegar, tunneling fifty yards into the solid rock.

At last, their iron chisels broke through into a dark, echoing ascending passage paved with polished granite.

Al-Ma'mun and his chief scholars crawled through the narrow passage, their torches illuminating immense vaulted galleries, until they entered the King’s Chamber in the heart of the pyramid. The air was cold and ancient. In the center stood a single, plain sarcophagus carved of solid dark granite, completely empty!

There were neither heaps of gold nor chests of rubies, only the silent, unyielding stone that had defied four thousand years of human storms.

Perceiving the disappointment of his exhausted workmen, Al-Ma'mun secretly ordered his treasurer to bury a purse of three hundred gold dinars in the floor of the passage. When the masons unearthed the purse, they rejoiced, finding that the gold exactly equaled the wages of their six months of labor!

Al-Ma'mun looked upon the colossal monument and smiled with philosophical humility: 'The ancients did not build this mountain of stone to hoard gold; they built it to teach the conquerors of the future that the monuments of pride endure longer than the empires that raised them.'
moral: Human ambition that seeks to conquer ancient stone learns that true greatness lies in preserving wisdom.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
